For the last few weeks, I've been building a new project called Loopy[dot]computer
Loopy is an orchestrator for event-driven agent workflows. Simply put, it's an easy way to define agent workflows that should run when your data changes.
Loopy is open source, agent-neutral, and code-first. You can version control your workflows, use whatever agent you prefer, and host in infra you control.
I've been thinking about the future of agent automations (and loops, much en vogue these past few weeks) for a long time and while my usual method of exploring ideas is to write, it's been pretty exhilarating to be back in the saddle and shipping serious code. It's been a minute.

There are different kinds of "loops" that help agents figure out what they should work on.
1. Event-driven: Systems process sensor data (customer feedback, bug reports, observability etc...) in ways that uncover work that agents need to perform in pursuit of well-defined objectives.
2. Explorers: Agents continuously investigate the search space of possible improvements in ways that reflect company goals, strategy, and taste.
3. Sims: Synthetic users navigate the product to unearth potential issues before customers see them.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Turning off-policy tokens on-policy in reinforcement learning for language models
summary:
"Turning Off-Policy Tokens On-Policy"
In LLM RL, generation is expensive, so you often reuse rollouts for multiple training steps. But by the time the model learns from those tokens, its policy has already changed. That means the token may no longer match what the current model would have chosen.
This paper, SIS, fixes this by testing each token. If it still looks like something the current model would sample, treat it as on-policy. If not, apply the usual correction.
So instead of just clipping noisy off-policy ratios, it turns many off-policy tokens back on-policy.
When this plugs into GRPO, DAPO, and GSPO, it improves math and agentic search, and makes training more stable under stale rollouts and MoE mismatch.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HM-0oYBXIAALxUM.jpg
clean_summary: In reinforcement learning with large language models, reuse of rollouts for multiple training steps can cause issues because the model's policy changes over time, making previously sampled tokens no longer align with the current policy. The SIS method addresses this by testing each token to see if it still matches what the current model would sample; if so, it treats the token as on-policy, otherwise it applies the usual correction. This approach effectively turns many off-policy tokens back on-policy, improving training stability and performance when integrated with methods like GRPO, DAPO, and GSPO, especially under stale rollouts and model mismatch conditions.

Why does RL improve reasoning after SFT?
This paper says SFT gives the model full worked solutions, but the useful pieces inside them are tangled together.
RL basically adds reward guided variation, which helps the model separate those pieces into reusable skills and routing rules.
Then the model can recombine them on problems it never saw during SFT.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HM-0uxAWoAA0obh.jpg
clean_summary: This paper explains that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides the model with full worked solutions, but the useful parts are tangled together. Reinforcement learning (RL) adds reward-guided variation, helping the model separate these parts into reusable skills and routing rules. As a result, the model can recombine these skills to solve problems it has never seen during SFT.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
My bet: in the near future, 80%⬆️ of CS research will be done by AI in collaboration with humans. However, today's research ecosystem is still built around the human, not the AI scientist.
For example, the 8-page paper PDF is a lossy compression of months of branching exploration into a linear story, optimized for a human reviewer to skim in 30 minutes. It hides two structural taxes:
📖 Storytelling Tax — failures, rejected hypotheses, and dead ends get stripped. On RE-Bench (24,008 runs, 21 frontier models), failed runs = 90.2% of total compute cost, with a 113× median failed-to-success token ratio. Every lab independently rediscovers the same dead ends.
🔧 Engineering Tax — the gap between reviewer-sufficient prose and agent-sufficient spec. Across 8,921 PaperBench requirements (23 ICML'24 papers), only 45.4% are fully specified in the PDF. The rest is tacit lab knowledge. Tolerable when readers were human. Critical now that agents read, reproduce, and extend.
We propose ARA: the Agent-Native Research Artifact — replace the narrative PDF with an agent-executable package, in 4 layers:
🧠 structured scientific logic
⚙️ executable code w/ full specs
🌳 exploration graph (every failure preserved)
📊 evidence grounding every claim

summary:
“Towards Mechanistically Understanding Why Memorized Knowledge Fails to Generalize in LLM Finetuning”
LLMs can quickly memorize new facts during fine-tuning, but still fail when those facts need to be used in multi-hop reasoning.
This paper shows the issue is not missing knowledge, but knowledge–circuit misalignment. The fact exists inside the model, just not in the layers where reasoning happens.
Their self-patching method moves the right hidden representation into the right layer and recovers much of the lost generalization, with a simple heuristic recovering 58-75% of oracle headroom.

clean_summary: Large language models can quickly memorize new facts during fine-tuning but still struggle to use those facts in multi-hop reasoning. This issue is not due to missing knowledge but rather a misalignment between knowledge and the reasoning circuit within the model. The fact exists inside the model, just not in the layers where reasoning occurs. A self-patching method moves the relevant hidden representations into the correct layers, recovering much of the lost generalization. A simple heuristic can recover 58-75% of the potential improvement.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Separating state prediction and next-token prediction in transformers
summary:
"The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis"
Transformers use the same hidden state to both predict the next token and store memory for future tokens, which may force two competing jobs into one representation, and may be wasting data by mixing memory and prediction in the same computation.
This paper splits them into two streams, input tokens for persistent state and predict tokens for next-token prediction.
Across 53M to 1.7B params, this approach achieves lower loss, 2 to 3 point downstream gains, and at 1.6B matches a standard Transformer trained on 47B tokens with only 18B tokens.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNJe5CbXMAA-kpG.jpg
clean_summary: Transformers typically use the same hidden state to predict the next token and store memory for future tokens, which may cause these two tasks to compete and lead to inefficiencies. Splitting them into two streams—one for persistent memory and one for next-token prediction—reduces loss and improves downstream performance across models from 53 million to 1.7 billion parameters. At 1.6 billion parameters, this approach matches the performance of a standard Transformer trained on 47 billion tokens using only 18 billion tokens, demonstrating a more efficient use of data.

New in-depth blog post time: "Inside TPU and GPU Clusters: The Anatomy of Collective Communication".

summary:
“Qwen-Music Technical Report”
AI music generation has to solve two problems at once, composing a coherent song and rendering it as high-fidelity audio.
This Qwen paper however splits them apart.
Qwen-Music first plans music in compact 25 Hz semantic tokens, uses Melody-CoT to reason over melody, then renders the result into 48 kHz stereo audio.
This creates a single model for prompt-to-song and cover generation that beats or matches top proprietary systems across most objective and human evals.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNTPR-xWYAACWIz.jpg
clean_summary: AI music generation faces two main challenges: composing a coherent song and rendering it as high-fidelity audio. The Qwen-Music approach separates these tasks by first planning music in compact 25 Hz semantic tokens, then using Melody-CoT to reason over the melody, and finally rendering the music into 48 kHz stereo audio. This results in a single model capable of prompt-to-song and cover generation that outperforms or matches top proprietary systems across most objective and human evaluations.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Requential Coding: Pushing the Limits of Model Compression with Self-Generated Training Data"
This paper, Requential Coding, compresses models by coding what they learn, not their weights.
So a student trains on samples it generates itself. A teacher then only points out which samples are useful, which means the code only pays when teacher and student disagree.
This makes compression ignore model size and raw data noise.
And the results are surprising. They found that bigger models can need fewer bits at the same loss, and this gives stronger generalization bounds for scaled LLMs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNTPdokWgAAr-2D.jpg

🚀New paper on Looped Transformers!
Latent reasoning is fast, but struggles to match CoT-level accuracy at scale. Can looped Transformers give us both?
We find: yes! A looped padded backbone turns out to be a surprisingly simple recipe that works -- It gives latent thoughts a parallel workspace that can be supervised similarly to explicit CoT. 🧵

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
Some fun techniques for mitigating context rot in long-horizon search!
Quoting @ShijieX60925
🔥 Announcing our new paper: "Diagnosing and Mitigating Context Rot in Long-horizon Search"
Extensive context has become the norm as LLMs are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks such as deep search. However, it remains unclear how models behave given extensive context in such scenarios, and how different strategies can alleviate the resulting issues.
Our work reveals a prevalent but previously unnoticed phenomenon: as the accumulated context grows, agents directly give up or prematurely hand over uncertain answers, and it gets worse the longer they run. We diagnose why this happens and show how to mitigate it through context management and rejection sampling.
📈 Key Findings:
1️⃣ Across 4 flagship models and 3 benchmarks, extensive context drives a sharp rise in "give-up" and "uncertain" errors. The context window itself is NOT the bottleneck.
2️⃣ Rot is caused by the accumulated content, not merely trajectory length or turn count. Wiping all context nearly eliminates rot but explodes unfinished trajectories, so careful management beats brute-force deletion.
3️⃣ Systematically comparing 7 context management methods, combining compaction + trimming achieves the best cost-rot balance, while sub-agent isolation can win big but is highly model-dependent.
4️⃣ Rot-aware rejection sampling delivers a 2.6%-4.9% average gain, with the biggest wins where rot is most severe.

clean_title: Concurrent image understanding and generation with self-correcting coupled Markov jump processes
summary:
"Concurrent Image Understanding and Generation: Self-Correcting Coupled Markov Jump Processes"
Google's CO2Jump lets a model understand and edit an image at the same time.
So instead of first writing text and then generating pixels, text and image tokens update together during diffusion.
The key here is self-correction. If the text or image makes a bad early guess, CO2Jump can remask it and revise it using cross-modal attention.
So the model does not just generate. It negotiates between what it sees, what it says, and what it draws.
This improves joint image editing, maze solving, and nonogram solving, where the text and image must agree.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2078483911395459072/img/1grnXP67v2zvnMna.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2078483911395459072/vid/avc1/484x270/EvRlgpK7ylOANcOq.mp4?tag=29

Instead of first generating text and then pixels, text and image tokens are updated together during diffusion. The key is self-correction: if the model makes a bad early guess, CO2Jump can remask and revise it using cross-modal attention. This enables better joint image editing, maze solving, and nonogram solving, where text and image must be consistent.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Xiaomi's production deployment of hybrid SWA for long-context inference
summary:
Hybrid SWA can make long-context inference ~7x cheaper in theory.
And this paper shows how Xiaomi made it work in production for MiMo-V2.5.
The main trick is fixing the KV cache system so SWA only stores the recent window, not the full context, while still reusing prefixes safely across requests.
With better cache routing, distributed caching, and multimodal preprocessing, they were able to get 93%+ KV cache hit rates, ~40% faster prefill, ~5x more decode KV capacity, and 2x encoder throughput.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNhCUj4XIAAasxZ.jpg

By improving cache routing, distributed caching, and multimodal preprocessing, they achieved over 93% KV cache hit rates, about 40% faster prefill, roughly 5 times more decode KV capacity, and doubled encoder throughput.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies”
Most robot policies only see the current moment, so they struggle with long tasks where past actions matter.
This paper gives robots long context by updating fast weights during inference, turning rollout history into a compact memory instead of a huge attention window.
With 8K timesteps of context, RoboTTT imitates from one human video, recovers from mistakes, and finishes a five-minute assembly task no baseline completes.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNo8IILXgAAnei8.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: On-Policy delta distillation for reasoning-focused model training
summary:
"On-Policy Delta Distillation"
So instead of copying everything a teacher model prefers, this paper asks what changed after the teacher learned reasoning.
It compares the reasoning-tuned teacher to its base model, then distills that difference into the student.
This focuses training on reasoning-specific behavior, not the teacher’s generic style or old pretraining habits.
This approach gives better math, code, and science reasoning across Qwen3 and Gemma4, especially where normal on-policy distillation can hurt strong models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNo8-a6XcAAvemv.jpg
clean_summary: On-Policy Delta Distillation is a method that focuses on training a student model to learn the reasoning improvements of a teacher model. Instead of copying the teacher's preferred outputs, it compares the reasoning-tuned teacher to its base model and distills that difference into the student. This technique enhances math, code, and science reasoning in models like Qwen3 and Gemma4, especially where standard on-policy distillation can degrade performance.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Loop the Loopies!"
This paper Loopie shows recurrent Transformers can be compute efficient, not just parameter efficient.
Contrast to how we love stacking more layers, they have each MoE layer loops twice before moving on. This actually saves activation memory, improves throughput, and reinvests the gain into capacity.
Their Loopie-20B-A2B using this approach beats a compute-matched vanilla 30B-A3B MoE baseline, with only 2B active params, and reaches gold-level IMO/IPhO performance without tools.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNsZVm6XQAAxpbz.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"T²MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence"
T²MLR adds recurrence where Transformers seem to reason best, which is the middle layers.
So it caches a middle-layer state from the previous token and feeds it into the next token, avoiding the token-space bottleneck.
By only recurring through 20% of layers, it can beat full recurrence, improves reasoning, and can retrofit a 1.7B model with little inference overhead.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNsZakkXkAA8b3c.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Transformers generalize through composition via harness design
summary:
Transformers struggle to generalize to tasks they were not explicitly trained on. Instead, we propose in 2026 that it is the job of the harness to generalize through composition.
We observe a powerful property when training RLMs: for tasks with shared structure that look different, the root model naturally learns the same trajectory, meaning it views the two task trajectories as the same! In other words, the Transformer does not need additional generalization capabilities to transfer capabilities from one task to the other, the harness induces it.
We find that well-designed harnesses form a quotient set over task trajectories, meaning their individual LLM calls can see structurally “similar” tasks as near-identical, token-for-token! Harnesses can effectively generalize for the Transformer during training, without relying on any intrinsic generalization capability from the model.
For example, RLMs can see problems of different lengths as the same: we show that RLMs can train exclusively on short tasks, and fully generalize to similar but unseen tasks 8-32x longer because it produces near identical trajectories for both.
Taking this further, we show that tasks across different domains (e.g. math solutions vs. essay writing) that share a decomposition strategy exhibit the same generalization effect. RLMs can train on the problem of finding which essays belong to the same author and improve performance on finding math problems that share similar solutions.
The full blogpost, experiments, and discussion are in the thread below.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNrQLbwXwAAyU4j.jpg
clean_summary: Transformers often struggle to generalize to tasks they were not explicitly trained on. Instead, it is proposed that the harness should enable generalization through composition. When training recurrent language models (RLMs), tasks with shared structure that appear different are viewed as the same trajectory by the root model, meaning the model does not need intrinsic generalization capabilities. Well-designed harnesses form a quotient set over task trajectories, allowing the model to treat structurally similar tasks as nearly identical, token-for-token. This enables RLMs trained on short tasks to generalize to much longer, similar tasks by producing near-identical trajectories. Furthermore, tasks across different domains that share a decomposition strategy also benefit, with models trained on one domain improving performance in another. The work suggests that the harness, rather than the model itself, induces the ability to generalize through composition.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Language model harnesses are compositional generalizers"
The current frontier LLM landscape feels like an endless hunger for more data, longer contexts, and harder tasks.
But with Recursive LMs, context can be offloaded and sub-agents can be called, so the main model technically sees many different tasks as the same simple structure.
This paper uses that idea and trains the model on shorter tasks, while still generalizing to tasks 8-32x longer.
Each step stays locally in-distribution, even when the full task is much longer or comes from a different domain.
The model also learns the reusable decomposition pattern behind the task, instead of just memorizing the task itself.
So basically, they reframed generalization as a harness design problem, not just a more data and longer context problem. Fascinating idea.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Using world modeling to create better language agents
summary:
I just published my blog on using world modeling to create better language agents. Here are the key takeaways…
Link to the blog:
How does this work? Although RL provides sparse rewards, agent trajectories are information-rich. Every interaction contains both an agent action and the resulting environment observation. Standard agentic RL discards these observations during training. Recent work instead uses observations as a dense source of supervision by augmenting RL with a world modeling objective. RL is applied to LLM-generated action tokens, while SFT is applied to observation tokens.
World modeling as a learning objective. RL teaches agents which actions maximize reward, while world modeling teaches how the environment responds to those actions. Rather than optimizing these objectives independently, recent work jointly trains them with only minor modifications to standard RL. This improves sample efficiency, agent performance, and generalization.
Environment supervision. Environment observations provide valuable supervision, even from low-reward trajectories, because they describe the consequences of an agent's actions. However, not every observation is useful. Recent methods filter repetitive failures, invalid tool calls, and other low-information observations so that training focuses on signals that improve an agent's understanding of the environment.
Overfitting. We must be careful with how world modeling is incorporated into the RL objective. If the world modeling loss is weighted too heavily, the agent may prioritize environment prediction over learning reward-maximizing behavior. Because world modeling provides dense supervised feedback, it may also overfit more quickly than pure RL. Overfitting is particularly pronounced in retrieval-heavy environments (e.g., web search), where world modeling may encourage memorization. To solve these issues, we must:
- Carefully balance the world modeling weight relative to RL.
- Normalize the objectives separately to ensure comparable magnitude.
- Use data filtering, tool selection, or early stopping to prevent overfitting.
Overfitting typically appears later in training, where held-out performance drops despite rising training rewards.
Cost and scalability. World modeling is straightforward to implement and can be incorporated into existing agentic RL systems with relatively little overhead. Unified training approaches for RL and world modeling typically reuse information that is already present in the rollouts for RL to compute the world modeling loss. The only additional cost is the added sum over observation token log probabilities to compute the supervised loss. Incorporating the world modeling loss into RL also tends to improve training efficiency.
Agent capabilities. Beyond benchmark gains, world modeling enables agents to:
- Use tools more effectively.
- Require fewer expert demonstrations.
- Better leverage inference-time compute.
- Generalize more reliably to new environments.
Overall, world modeling provides a simple, practical way to improve agent training by helping LLM agents build a deeper understanding of the environments in which they operate.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNranFxWoAApJKp.jpg

A blog discusses how incorporating world modeling into reinforcement learning can improve language agents. Standard RL uses sparse rewards and discards environment observations, but recent approaches augment RL with a world modeling objective, training agents to predict environment responses alongside maximizing rewards. This joint training enhances sample efficiency, performance, and generalization, while also enabling agents to use tools more effectively, require fewer demonstrations, and better leverage inference compute.

Care must be taken to balance the world modeling loss to prevent overfitting, especially in retrieval-heavy environments. The method is straightforward to implement and adds minimal overhead, reusing existing rollout information to compute the supervised loss. Overall, world modeling helps agents develop a deeper understanding of their environments, leading to more capable and reliable language agents.

clean_title: Looped Transformer model improves latent reasoning speed and accuracy
summary:
"Bridging the Gap Between Latent and Explicit Reasoning with Looped Transformers"
Latent reasoning lets models think without writing every reasoning step, but it usually loses accuracy as models get bigger.
This paper, LOTUS, fixes this by using a looped Transformer that updates many hidden thoughts in parallel, then trains them to match real CoT steps.
So the model gets CoT-like reasoning without generating the full CoT.
At 3B, it nearly matches explicit CoT on GSM8K while thinking 2.5x faster, and 6.9x faster for long reasoning.
The hidden thoughts can also be read back as reasoning steps, making them compressed but not completely ambiguous.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNx33CRXwAAm8mg.jpg

The LOTUS model addresses this by using a looped Transformer that updates many hidden thoughts in parallel and trains them to match real chain-of-thought steps. This enables the model to perform chain-of-thought-like reasoning without generating full explanations. At 3B parameters, it nearly matches explicit chain-of-thought on GSM8K while thinking 2.5 times faster, and 6.9 times faster for longer reasoning tasks. The study finds that more pretraining tokens lead to faster RL improvements, and while RL sharpens easy cases, it can also uncover correct moves in challenging scenarios.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
World Modeling with JEPA has recently gained traction thanks to a novel anti-collapse mechanism called "SIGReg" (by @ylecun and @randall_balestr). The math is clean, but it is rarely explained from first principles, so I broke it down in a detailed blog post 📰
Here is the summary (🧵):
The problem: in JEPA, both sides of the prediction loss go through the same encoder. Map every input to a single constant point, the predictor matches it trivially, and the loss hits exactly zero. Perfect score, zero information. Gradient descent finds this solution by default.
Prior work patched around it with stop-gradients, EMA teacher-student models, frozen pretrained encoders, and VICReg-style losses with 6+ hand-tuned coefficients. Each adds instability, hyperparameters, or a dependency on someone else's pretraining.
---
SIGReg replaces all of that with one regularizer built on a single claim: force the batch of embeddings to look like samples from an isotropic Gaussian, N(0, I). LeJEPA proves this isn't arbitrary. It's the distribution that minimizes worst-case downstream risk across linear and nonlinear probes.
But "make the embeddings Gaussian" is easy to say and hard to compute. You can't estimate a density in 200+ dimensions from a small batch. The fix is a chain of four classical results: compare Fourier transforms instead of densities, turn that comparison into a single scalar, approximate the integral with ~16 points, and lift the whole thing from 1D to any dimension with a theorem from 1936. Each step is simple. The stack is what makes it work. Read the subsequent posts in this thread to understand each step.
---
But why it provably works: the only distribution for which SIGReg = 0 is N(0, I), which is full rank by construction, with every eigenvalue equal to 1. A collapsed low-rank encoder cannot be a minimum. It's not just unlikely to converge there—it's mathematically excluded.
And the training loop stays boring:
total loss = prediction + λ·SIGReg
The encoder gets gradients from both terms; the predictor gets gradients from the prediction term only. No alternating updates, no stop-gradients, no two-timescale tricks.
Now check out the breakdown below. 👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HN6st85WkAAL9fv.jpg

clean_title: SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales
summary:
"SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales"
This new NVIDIA paper suggests that AdamW may not be sufficient for frontier LLM pretraining anymore!
In the paper, they show that higher-order optimizers like Muon and SOAP can train large LLMs more efficiently at extreme batch sizes, up to 100M tokens, where AdamW starts losing stability and token efficiency.
The reason why is that AdamW rescales each weight independently, while Muon and SOAP respect the matrix structure of neural network layers. That makes a huge difference in terms of learning more efficiently.
They also fixed SOAP’s large-scale instability with per-step QR eigenbasis updates, current-gradient preconditioning, and KL-Shampoo covariance estimation, then make these optimizers work inside Megatron-LM with a layer-wise distributed optimizer.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOAmmeqXEAArizO.jpg

The reason is that AdamW rescales each weight independently, while Muon and SOAP respect the matrix structure of neural network layers. This makes a significant difference in learning efficiency. title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Beyond Euclidean Clipping: Overcoming Exploration Collapse in LLM RL via Riemannian Isometric Policy Optimization"
PPO-Clip is the default for LLM RL, but it accidentally kills exploration by treating all probability ratio changes as equally large.
This paper shows the bug is geometric. Rare tokens and common tokens live in very different parts of the policy manifold, so fixed clipping under-updates rare but useful reasoning paths and over-updates already dominant ones.
They fix this with probability-aware Riemannian clipping, giving rare actions more room and common actions less.
This gives smoother RL, less exploration collapse, and up to 60% better AIME24 performance over GRPO.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOAmtmUXAAA2qC9.jpg

clean_title: Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding in Neural Network Compression
summary:
“Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding”
Neural networks hide their knowledge in functions, but most compression methods look at raw weights, which are distorted by scale symmetries and architecture quirks.
This DeepMind paper, HOPE, moves compression into Hilbert function space, treating each neuron as a rank-1 operator.
It makes pruning, neuron merging, and residual block removal part of the same low-rank projection framework.
This gives a data-free, hyperparameter-free way to find which learned functions are redundant, and can easily expose the model’s core representation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOGHo36WYAAi4Tb.jpg

The DeepMind paper HOPE introduces a new approach by moving compression into Hilbert function space, treating each neuron as a rank-1 operator. This framework unifies pruning, neuron merging, and residual block removal as low-rank projections, providing a data-free, hyperparameter-free method to identify redundant learned functions and reveal the model's core representations.

clean_title: Context-weighted discrete flow matching improves diffusion models
summary:
"Context-weighted Discrete Flow Matching"
This paper makes discrete diffusion less blind to context.
Standard DFM treats every masked token the same, even though some are easy because nearby words are already known, while others are basically guesses.
So this paper’s key idea is to fill in the tokens that have more nearby context first, and give those tokens more weight during training.
That small change improves generation without extra cost or fine-tuning, cuts perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText, improves MAUVE by up to 24%, and helps generate many more valid molecules while still keeping flexible any-order generation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOGHuUoWQAAQyTK.jpg
clean_summary: This paper makes discrete diffusion less blind to context. Standard discrete flow matching (DFM) treats every masked token equally, but some tokens are easier to predict because their nearby words are known, while others are harder guesses. The key idea is to fill in tokens with more nearby context first and give those tokens more weight during training. This small change enhances generation quality without extra cost or fine-tuning, reducing perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText, increasing MAUVE by up to 24%, and enabling the generation of many more valid molecules while maintaining flexible, any-order generation.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Sample-efficient learning from agent experience via experience distillation
summary:
"Sample-Efficient Learning from Agent Experience"
Agents can learn from trial and error in context, but forget once the context is gone.
This paper propose something called Experience Distillation. So you let an experience-conditioned teacher look at old agent rollouts, ask it for the next decision at real history points, then train the student to make those decisions without the experience context.
No extra environment rollouts and no long synthetic trajectories needed, while also keeping up to 93.4% of ICL gains. It also matches RL baselines with at least 9.6x fewer environment samples.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOR-yn5XIAAIlPX.jpg
clean_summary: Agents can learn from trial and error in context, but tend to forget once the context is gone. This work proposes experience distillation, where an experience-conditioned teacher reviews old agent rollouts and provides next decisions at real history points, enabling the student to learn without needing extra environment rollouts or synthetic trajectories. This approach retains up to 93.4% of in-context learning gains and matches reinforcement learning baselines with at least 9.6 times fewer environment samples.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“PRO-LONG: Programmatic Memory Enables Long-Horizon Reasoning”
Long-horizon agents forget because their history gets too long, and summaries often throw away details that only matter later.
This paper keeps the full trajectory as a structured log, then lets the coding agent search it with grep, regex, and Python.
So memory becomes lossless and programmatic instead of compressed and heuristic.
On ARC-AGI-3, PRO-LONG improves base coding agents by 18 points on average, and uses 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens than specialized harnesses.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOViaj8WsAA9H9w.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: AREX: a recursive approach for self-improving research agents
summary:
“AREX: Towards a Recursively Self-Improving Agent for Deep Research”
Deep research agents often fail not because they need more search, but because they don’t know which parts of an answer are already verified and which constraints are still unresolved.
This paper turns research into a recursive loop: answer, verify constraint-by-constraint, preserve evidence, then refine only the weak parts.
AREX adds learned context updates and step-aware RL, achieving extremely strong results with 4B and 122B-A10B models across various agentic benchmarks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOVifcOWQAAA4MP.jpg
clean_summary: Deep research agents often struggle not because they need more search, but because they cannot distinguish verified parts of an answer from unresolved constraints. This approach turns research into a recursive loop: answer, verify constraints individually, preserve evidence, and refine only the weak parts. AREX enhances this process with learned context updates and step-aware reinforcement learning, achieving strong results with models up to 122B parameters across various benchmarks.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
Hindsight is 20/20 and it turns out you can train your agents with it.
We used an ensemble of GPT-5.6-Sol and Fable 5 research agents to run a small-scale replication of “Sample-Efficient Learning from Agent Experience.” The agents post-trained Qwen3.5-9B with Tinker on SWE-smith tasks using the Experience to Policy Distillation (EPD) technique introduced in the paper.
EPD distills an experience-conditioned teacher (opposed to a solution-conditioned one) into a student model
We found that EPD captures 44.1% of the in-context learning gains, corroborating the paper’s headline claim. Vanilla SFT captured 0%.
Two additional ablations surprised us:
- SFT on only each task’s final, successful trial scored lower than ordinary SFT on all trials
- Using four sampled teacher sequences per trial instead of one underperformed both with matched optimization steps and with proportionally more training

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"LeRoPE: Learnable RoPE Frequencies Improve Language Modeling"
LLMs use hand-picked RoPE frequencies to understand token positions, but this paper shows they work better when the frequencies are learned.
With just 32 extra parameters, LeRoPE beats RoPE across scales and discovers a dominant positional band around 2.2x the training context.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOapvM7XIAA9XwJ.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization”
LLMs often waste inference compute by restarting failed reasoning from scratch, even when most of the prefix was correct.
This paper lets the model use feedback to find the exact token where its reasoning broke, then branch from there instead of regenerating everything.
TTEL gets higher pass@k with far fewer tokens, using about half the token cost of independent sampling.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOapz17WYAIQell.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Weak-to-Strong on-policy distillation improves frontier models
summary:
“Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation”
Strong models usually need stronger teachers for OPD, and that is hard to come by for frontier models.
So this paper shows you can improve a strong model using weaker models by distilling the logit direction between a weak positive and weaker negative model, not copying either one.
Post-RL minus pre-RL, 4B minus 0.6B, and correct hint minus wrong hint all create useful proxy teachers.
In their result, Qwen3-8B improves on math and code, and sometimes surpassing the 4B RL teacher it learns from too.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOfogjDW4AEpwEp.jpg
clean_summary: Strong models often require stronger teachers for on-policy distillation, which can be hard to find for frontier models. This approach improves a strong model by distilling the logit direction between a weaker positive and an even weaker negative model, rather than copying either one. Using proxies like post-RL minus pre-RL, 4B minus 0.6B, and correct hint minus wrong hint, the method enables smaller models to learn effectively. Results show that Qwen3-8B improves on math and code tasks, sometimes surpassing the RL teacher it learns from.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Living-Harness: an interactive-agent evolver that learns procedural repairs
summary:
“Living-Harness Is an Interactive-Agent Evolver”
LLM agents can recover inside one task, but they often forget the fix after the episode ends.
So this paper propose the idea of having the agent harness evolve. Evaluator feedback is converted into episodic memory and a state graph, so failures become reusable procedural repairs.
Tools stay frozen, but the workflow learns when to trigger a repair, what action was missing, and how to recover next time.
It gets about +10 Pass@1 over the strongest interactive baselines on τ²-Bench and MultiWOZ-2.4.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOfopU2XoAA1sjK.jpg
clean_summary: LLM agents can recover within a single task, but they often forget the fix after the episode ends. This work proposes having the agent's harness evolve by converting evaluator feedback into episodic memory and a state graph, making failures reusable procedural repairs. Tools remain frozen, but the workflow learns when to trigger a repair, what action was missing, and how to recover next time. It achieves about a 10% improvement in Pass@1 over the strongest interactive baselines on τ²-Bench and MultiWOZ-2.4.

summary:
The new Pangram-4 Tech report is out. Some cool details on how to train a SOTA AI-text classifier:
The backbone is an undisclosed “popular open-weight MoE”. Speculating here, but think Mistral Small 4 / Qwen3.5-122B-A10B scale

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
We discovered a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data: exploration.
Scaling exploration monotonically improves existing models across images/video/language, and unlocks end-to-end generation.
In the simplest case, it's just a for loop.
Introducing Explorative Modeling.
TLDR:
- Gains from exploration grow with scale: 7%→36% as data scales, 13%→23% as parameters scale, and gains double at 3× the compute
- Adding exploration to ~SOTA baselines improves data efficiency by 6.2×, FLOP efficiency by 4.1×, parameter efficiency by 47%, and hits a near-SOTA 1.43 unguided FID on ImageNet
- Exploration lets you trade training compute for generalization, and scales how end-to-end your generative model is
- End-to-end Explorative Models (XMs) match diffusion performance on control tasks with up to 256× less inference compute
🧵Thread:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOkaQJRboAAlFAP.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Metis: Memory foundation model with integrated persistent memory
summary:
"Metis: Memory Foundation Model"
Most AI agents still use memory as an external RAG-style module, so the model retrieves old text instead of actually remembering.
This paper makes memory native to the Transformer. So past interactions are compressed into dynamic layer states and read through memory attention during normal forward passes.
The model weights stay frozen at inference, but its memory state updates without gradients, giving the model persistent memory inside the backbone.
Still early and lossy, but this is yet another paper with a big step toward agents that remember natively instead of outsourcing memory to a database.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOk1xKIXAAAhcP6.jpg
clean_summary: Most AI agents still use memory as an external RAG-style module, retrieving old text instead of actually remembering. This paper introduces Metis, a memory-native Transformer where past interactions are compressed into dynamic layer states and accessed via memory attention during normal forward passes. The model weights remain frozen at inference, but its memory state updates without gradients, enabling the model to have persistent memory inside the backbone. Although still early and lossy, this represents a significant step toward agents that remember natively instead of relying on external databases.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Wonder: Video World Model Done Better”
This paper from Adobe Research fixes some key issues from World Models like drifting controls, fading memories, and latency growth with context by co-designing camera control, memory, and distillation.
Wonder turns camera motion into pixel-space visual cues, keeps full-fidelity history while sparsely retrieving only relevant chunks, and distills into a real-time student that still follows the camera.
They were able to achieve minute-scale interactive world exploration at 16 FPS from images or videos.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOk11f6WIAAOjWt.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation"
Explorative Modeling argues generative models have been missing a third scaling axis.
We scale parameters and data, but not generative expressivity, the number of modes a training objective can preserve instead of averaging into blur.
The core idea is simple. During training, generate K candidates and backprop only through the one closest to the data. This factors the training loop instead of the generation process. And that lets models commit to different modes while making generation more end-to-end.
The results are surprisingly strong too. This includes 4.1x better FLOP efficiency, 1.43 unguided ImageNet FID, 6.2x better sample efficiency, 47% better parameter efficiency across diffusion, flow, video, image, and masked diffusion LMs.
On top of that, diffusion-level control got 16 to 256x fewer inference steps.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOk6L3_WgAAj2Bm.jpg

clean_summary:
Cleaning large language model pretraining data is often done with hand-crafted rules based on noisy text and fixed pipelines, which can be inefficient and inconsistent. The idea is to let a model learn to determine the best cleaning method for each individual piece of text automatically.

DataOrchestra is a system that enables models to figure out the appropriate data cleaning recipe on a per-example basis, reducing reliance on manual priors and fixed procedures. The linked arXiv paper presents the approach, and the GitHub repository provides the implementation.

A new paper explores how inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) can help align AI systems by having them imitate human behavior. The question is whether expert demonstrations alone can produce an explicit, inspectable reward signal for alignment without needing preference labels or external verifiers.

The work demonstrates that IRL can change the AI alignment paradigm by deriving reward functions directly from human demonstrations, potentially simplifying the alignment process. The paper provides a method to learn these rewards and shows promising results, suggesting a new way to make AI systems better aligned with human values.

This 35B AI4AI agent is trained to improve ML solutions through executable evolution.
Rather than generating one ML pipeline, it evolves many candidates by drafting, refining, repairing, and recombining code. It then executes each in a sandbox, and learns from real task scores to guide longer-horizon search.

Suggesting that agents need environments with consequences, not just screenshots.

summary:
"Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers"
This paper from Adobe Research called Chimera is a Chinchilla-scaled hybrid DiT for long-context visual generation.
It replaces most full attention with KDA linear attention, adds periodic MLA for global token mixing, uses modality-aware short convs for spatiotemporal locality, and MoE for sparse capacity.
They then makes the heterogeneous backbone scale predictably across width and depth.
Result is 7.3x fewer FLOPs than Wan 2.1 2B to reach the same loss, plus zero-shot 5s to 30s video extrapolation without length finetuning.
Read more here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOvyoPdXwAATVNR.jpg

The model scales predictably across width and depth, resulting in 7.3 times fewer FLOPs than Wan 2.1 2B to reach the same loss, and enabling zero-shot 5 to 30-second video extrapolation without length finetuning. This architecture aims to efficiently handle token-intensive visual inputs.

summary:
"Reusing Rollouts under Policy Lag"
LLM RL wastes a lot of compute generating rollouts. So people reuse the same rollouts for multiple updates, but the model keeps changing, which makes old rollouts increasingly off-policy.
This paper suggests a better way to think about that mismatch, where you don’t just ask how likely the current token is now, you also ask how likely the prefix was that got the model to this token in the first place.
The exact prefix correction is too unstable because it multiplies ratios across many tokens. PNPO uses the prefix geometric mean instead, keeping the causal prefix signal while avoiding exploding weights.
This makes rollout reuse safer when policy lag gets larger.

This work proposes a better way to handle that mismatch by considering not only the likelihood of the current token but also the likelihood of the prefix that led to it. Instead of using the unstable prefix ratio, it employs the prefix geometric mean, which preserves the causal prefix signal while preventing exploding weights. This approach makes rollout reuse safer when policy lag increases. In experiments, PNPO outperforms GSPO by 3 points on average at a sequence length of 32 and achieves similar performance with only 150 rollout batches compared to 600, demonstrating improved efficiency and stability.

summary:
"The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does"
In factored models, the same solution can be written in many hidden bases.
Gradient descent treats those hidden bases as equivalent, so it keeps the usual low-rank bias.
But Adam does not. Its per-coordinate updates depend on the chosen basis, even when the model and loss are identical.
Which is why Adam can fit the training data perfectly but land on a worse, higher-rank solution.

RLSVR extends RLVR beyond math and code by making rewards verifiable through task transformation.

This converts subjective output quality into a self-generated RL signal without reward models or external judges.

summary:
"Model Discovery Agent: LLM-assisted Bayesian experiment design for data-efficient discovery of mechanistic world models"
This paper's Model Discovery Agent combines LLM hypothesis generation with Bayesian experimental design for mechanistic world-model discovery.
How it works is that an LLM proposes possible mechanisms, Bayesian SMC tracks which ones are plausible, and value-of-information chooses the next intervention where those mechanisms disagree most.
If none explain the new data, the LLM proposes new mechanisms and the loop repeats.
This creates a system that learns a causal and mechanistic world models with far fewer experiments.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPt1sqdXsAAJ_p_.jpg

summary:
"Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding"
Across 1,867 repos, CLAUDE.md-style files grow +226% because adding instructions is cheap, but deleting them gets riskier as their rationale is forgotten.
The older an instruction gets, the less likely anyone is to delete it because the reason it was added is increasingly hard to recover.
Their fix is simple: save why each instruction was added, so future maintainers know when it is safe to remove.
That let them eliminate 99.3% of unnecessary instructions and improve real-world instruction-following by up to 23.1%.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPt2w3_WsAAedXR.jpg

summary:
"Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation"
Self-improving agents usually learn from experience through a teacher that gets extra information, but humans still have to decide how that experience should be represented.
This paper makes that representation learnable. Past trajectories are compressed into latent context that helps the model become a better teacher for itself on the exact states the student visits.
The student then distills that guidance into its own weights, so the extra context is only needed for training, while still improving tool use and coding with much fewer rollouts.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HP5nu1jWEAAYhr9.jpg

This work makes the representation learnable by compressing past trajectories into a latent context that helps the model become a better teacher for itself on the states it visits. The student then distills this guidance into its own weights, so the extra context is only needed during training, enabling improvements in tool use and coding with fewer rollouts. The framework introduces a learnable latent representation for self-distillation, moving beyond fixed, human-engineered artifacts.

summary:
"Maglev: Sliding Recurrent Memory"
Transformers can either keep the full history with expensive attention, or use a sliding window that is efficient but forgets anything that falls outside it.
This paper makes that forgotten history recurrent. So they used a stronger prefiller that creates memory targets in parallel, and a sliding-window Transformer that learns to reproduce and carry those memories forward through its KV cache.
The prefiller is then removed at inference, so the model gets persistent nonlinear memory with fixed-size attention and KV cache, while still being trained with parallel Transformer passes.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQB2RUbW0AAhUFt.jpg

summary:
"LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure"
What happens if you train an LLM that has only ever seen elementary school knowledge?
This paper trains a 5B model from scratch on 88B tokens filtered to K-5 content, creating an explicit boundary around what the model was exposed to during pretraining.
Scaling, few-shot prompting, and even SFT + GRPO improve capabilities within that boundary, but do little for genuinely out-of-scope reasoning.
This gave insights on how pretraining exposure may set a much harder capability ceiling than we think, with post-training mostly amplifying what the model already learned rather than creating entirely new capabilities.

clean_title: Scaling Properties of Text Conditioning in Visual Generation
summary:
For years, text-to-image generation has scaled models, data, and compute. Yet every training image still reaches the model through a caption, which determines what visual information can be associated with text.
Can caption information itself be measured and scaled?
Introducing Scaling Properties of Text Conditioning in Visual Generation.
The demo shows the complete user prompt -> reasoning -> structured prompt -> image pipeline.
TL;DR:
- Longer natural-language prompts do not reliably provide more useful supervision.
- GPG and ED quantify image-grounded caption information and predict converged diffusion loss.
- We decompose generation quality as Diffusability × Promptability: how much usable information a representation exposes to the diffuser, and how well an LLM instantiates it from a user request.
- Structured prompts raise diffusability; LLM scale and post-training raise promptability.
- Together, higher diffusability and promptability improve composition, reasoning, and world-knowledge generation.
📄 Paper:
🌐 Project:
💻 Code:
🤗 Models:
🎬 Demo: https://t.co/HgvjPOEpiE
🧵 Thread below.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HOzhmDeaEAA5SO1.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/HOzhmDeaEAA5SO1.mp4
clean_summary:
Text-to-image generation has advanced by scaling models, data, and compute, but each training image still depends on a caption that influences what visual information is associated with text. This raises the question of whether caption information itself can be measured and scaled.

The work introduces metrics like GPG and ED to quantify how much caption information grounded in images contributes to the diffusion process and predicts the convergence of diffusion loss. It decomposes generation quality into Diffusability, how much useful information a prompt exposes to the model, and Promptability, how well an LLM can instantiate the prompt from user input. Structured prompts increase diffusability, while larger LLMs and post-training improve promptability. Combining higher diffusability and promptability enhances the model's ability to generate complex, reasoning, and knowledge-based outputs.

The findings suggest that structured prompts and larger models can improve visual generation by better leveraging the information in text prompts, independent of prompt length, and highlight the importance of prompt design and model scaling in visual AI systems.

summary:
"Recirculation"
Recirculation gives a pretrained Transformer a kind of working memory at inference time, without retraining.
So instead of letting useful context get buried in deeper layers, it feeds a small part of that information back into earlier layers as the model reads the next token.
This helps the model keep track of what it already understood. On Gemma3, it cuts perplexity by 23% and boosts GSM8K accuracy by 21%, with almost no extra generation latency.
Suggesting that better memory may already exist within pretrained models, and recirculation simply gives it a way to persist.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQH4NTpX0AAKMCu.jpg

It feeds a small part of the context back into earlier layers as the model processes each token, helping it remember what it has already understood. On Gemma3, this technique reduces perplexity by 23% and increases GSM8K accuracy by 21%, with almost no additional latency. This suggests that better memory capabilities may already exist within pretrained models, and recirculation offers a way to access and persist that memory.

summary:
“Mind Viruses: Self-Propagating Ideas in Multi-Agent LLM Systems”
The paper shows that once one agent picks up a bad idea, it can convince other agents to adopt it too, write it into persistent memory, and keep spreading it even after context resets, like a mind virus.
The scary part is that the failure can propagate socially through agent-to-agent communication instead of coming from a single prompt injection.
Harmful viruses spread less reliably and stronger models are often more resistant, but the key point is that agent-to-agent communication creates a new attack surface where misaligned goals can propagate through an entire system.

summary:
"Mathematics in the Age of AI"
In an age of abundant AI-generated proofs, human understanding may become more valuable than proof generation itself.
This new paper from Terence Tao argues that AI could make solving hard math problems much cheaper and faster, but at the same time, creates a new problem.
If AI can generate thousands of correct proofs, mathematicians can’t possibly read, understand, verify, and teach all of them.
So the scarce resource in mathematics shifts from finding proofs to making sense of them.
The important work becomes deciding which results matter, explaining the key ideas, connecting them to existing theory, and turning them into knowledge other mathematicians can actually use.

summary:
We’ve seen an explosion of new ML chips with unique architectural features, but software support remains the critical bottleneck
Achieving peak performance increasingly relies on hardware-specific optimizations in the kernels, but we observe that coding agents are particularly weak at this
Introducing Hawkeye, a framework that brings hardware-awareness to coding agents by grounding them in a minimal and comprehensive taxonomy of optimization strategies
For new GPU or ML accelerator architectures, you only need to write 10 unit tests and solution kernels (one per optimization strategy), and we show that coding agents can effectively scale test-time compute with this minimal supervision to write hardware-aware kernels
Hawkeye can port kernels across architectures (Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell), vendors (NVIDIA, AMD), and precisions (FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4) while consistently leveraging hardware features and approaching expert kernel performance
Work co-led with @keramakr and done in collaboration with Alexander Ingare @simonguozirui @18jeffreyma @ZishenW @simran_s_arora @Azaliamirh @profvjreddi

summary:
"On-Policy Self-Distillation in Diffusion Models"
Diffusion RL gets a reward only after the final image, even though the model actually acts through many intermediate denoising steps.
DiffusionOPSD turns that endpoint reward into explicit reward-improving targets at the model’s own intermediate states, then distills those targets back into the model and continually refreshes them on-policy.
Across two diffusion backbones and ten evaluators, it gets the best held-out score in 19 of 20 settings while cutting training GPU-hours by up to 63%.
The key idea is treating diffusion alignment less like noisy trajectory-level RL and more like continuously refreshed self-distillation with direct intermediate supervision.

clean_summary: A Stanford study analyzes nearly 250,000 real-world human-AI conversations with Claude to understand how people work with AI. It finds that AI is mainly used for augmentation rather than full automation, with 72% of conversations still led by humans. Users tend to engage more deeply as the stakes increase, and AI often serves as a teaching tool in 67% of relevant interactions. Friction occurs in about half of interactions but can be productive when users actively repair, challenge, or clarify the model’s output. The benefits of AI depend heavily on the human’s level of agency and critical engagement during interactions.
